title: Count the money
summary: Close the ledger for the soft open by hand: takings, every cost, profit, and what one hour of your own time earned. Repay the loan in real cash. Argue the reinvest, save or spend decision on paper before you make it. Then put the shop's code where a stranger could run a stand from it.
materials: the cash box exactly as it came home, and the float number you wrote down before the stand opened
every receipt, price and cost note from weeks 5, 6 and 7, including the ones you nearly threw away
the paper sale tally from Market Day, or the lines your tally program printed
two sheets of squared paper for the ledger, and a pen rather than a pencil
laptop with Python, the editor, and the season folder git has been watching since week 1
the parent-held GitHub account, with a parent signed in and sitting next to you
a grown up to receive the loan repayment and sign for it

steps.title: Ask, imagine, plan
steps.body:
The design loop, same six moves: ask, imagine, plan, build, test, fix. Today the thing you are building is a true account of what happened, and the test move is what makes it true.

Ask: how much did the shop actually make? Not how it felt. Not what was in the box at the end, which is your money and the float and possibly a note somebody handed you for something else. The question is what is left after every single cost is paid, and it has an exact answer that is waiting on the table in front of you.

Imagine: somebody who was not there, who likes you but is not on your side, reads your ledger and tries to find the hole in it. They ask where each number came from. Every line you cannot answer that question for is a line you made up. Write today so that person finds nothing.

Plan: four jobs in this order, and the order matters. One, the ledger, by hand, on paper, in pen. Two, the loan, repaid in real cash, counted out into a real hand. Three, the decision, argued on paper before it is made. Four, the shop's code goes public, with a README a stranger could run a stand from.

Two things worth saying out loud before you start. The first: the loan is not a cost. A cost is money that left and is not coming back. The loan is money that arrived and has to leave again. Keeping those two apart is most of what today teaches, and mixing them up is how the same borrowed money gets counted twice.

The second: in pen. A ledger written in pencil can be edited into whatever you wish had happened. If a line is wrong, rule one line through it, write the right number beside it, and leave the mistake showing. That is how real books are kept, and a crossing out that everyone can see is worth more than a clean page nobody can check.

Five minutes on your typing site. Home row first, then today's words until your fingers stop hunting: git, status, log, remote, origin, branch, main, push, README.

Then the row you have been avoiding all season: the numbers. Today is nothing but numbers, and hunting for the 7 costs you more time than any word does. Drill the digits 0 to 9 straight through, twice, without looking down. Then the two keys that go with them: the decimal point, and the minus sign for the costs.

Finish by typing the line git push -u origin main ten times. You will type it for real in about forty minutes, and a typo in it stops the whole thing dead.

figure.alt: Double entry asks the same amount to arrive by two routes: route one adds up the sale lines, route two counts the cash and subtracts the float. Agreement does not prove truth, but disagreement always finds a mistake.

steps.title: Double entry, a machine for catching your own lies
steps.body:
Here is a bookkeeping trick that is about five hundred years old and is still the reason banks work. A friar and mathematician called Luca Pacioli wrote it down in 1494, and the merchants of Venice were already using it before he did.

The trick is this: write every amount down twice, in two different places, and make the two places agree. Money that leaves the box is written once as money leaving, and once as the thing it bought. Money that arrives is written once as money arriving, and once as where it came from. Nothing is written down once.

Why bother? Because a number written once cannot be checked. If you write takings 96 and nothing else, there is no way on earth to tell whether it is right. But if takings have to arrive twice, by two different routes, then the two routes have to land on the same number, and if they do not, something is wrong. You have caught it, without anybody outside checking your work.

Your own two routes today are these. Route one: add up the sale lines from the tally. Route two: count the cash in the box and take away the float you counted before the stand opened. Both of them claim to be the takings. Write them both down before you look at whether they match.

And here is the honest part, which is the whole science moment. Double entry does not tell you the truth. It tells you when you do not have it. Two numbers that disagree prove there is a mistake, and say nothing at all about which one is wrong, so you go and look. Two numbers that agree are not a guarantee either: a sale you never typed and never took the money for is missing from both routes and both routes still agree. A check catches the mistakes it is shaped to catch, and no others, and knowing the shape of your own check is what stops you trusting it too far.

figure.alt: Thermal receipt paper is coated with a colourless dye and developer kept apart. The print head presses a grid of tiny heaters against the paper, and wherever it warms past about 70 C the two chemicals react and turn black, with no ink sprayed.

items.s: turns black only where heated, no ink sprayed

steps.title: Why a receipt goes dark without any ink
steps.body:
Every receipt from Market Day is thermal paper, and it never touched a drop of ink. It is coated with a dye and a separate chemical, both colourless, kept apart from each other. Heat lets them react and turn black exactly where it touched.

The printer inside a card reader does not spray anything. It presses a grid of tiny heating elements against the paper for a fraction of a second, warming only the dots it wants dark. That is why the print looks slightly grainy up close.

The reaction typically triggers a little above 70 C. Sunlight through a car window can heat a dashboard well past that temperature. A receipt left sitting on it can fog or blacken with no heater involved at all.

Test it gently: press a warm spoon, not a hot one, to a spare receipt corner. Watch the mark appear without a single drop of ink.

figure.alt: The ledger has two columns. Money in holds takings, counted two routes over, the loan and the float, each labelled in words so neither is mistaken for takings. Money out holds every cost. Profit is takings minus every cost; the loan and float are in neither side of that sum.

items.s: loan and float are on neither side of that sum

steps.title: Close the ledger
steps.body:
Squared paper, landscape, in pen. Two columns: money in on the left, money out on the right. Every line gets a date, what it was, and the amount. Nothing goes on the page that you cannot point at a receipt, a tally line or a counted coin for.

Money in has three kinds of line and they never mix. The takings, which the shop earned. The loan, which the family lent you at week 5 and which is not yours. And the float, the change money that went into the box before the first sale, which is not yours either. Label the loan line as a loan and the float line as a float, in words, so that nobody reading the page, including you in a month, can mistake either one for money the shop made.

Money out is every cost, and this is where ledgers get quietly wrong, because the small ones hide. Materials. The card and markers for tags and the sign. Anything you had to buy twice because the first one failed. The cost of the thing you broke in the bend test in week 5. If a cost was paid before the shop even had a name, it is still a cost. Go through week 5, 6 and 7 receipts one at a time and tick each one as you enter it, so none gets entered twice and none gets missed.

Now the takings, twice over, the way the science moment says. Route one: add the sale lines. Route two: count the cash in the box and subtract the float. Write both numbers down before you compare them. If they disagree, do not choose the one you like. Find out why: a sale served and never typed, change given wrong, a coin that rolled under the table, a float counted badly in week 7. Write what you found in the log, because the gap is a more interesting fact than the total.

Then the profit line: takings minus every cost. Neither the loan nor the float is in that sum, on either side. Write the sum out fully rather than the answer alone.

Last, the number the design cares about most. Add up the hours of your own time honestly: the Build hours, the making, the dressing, the rehearsal, the day itself, and the counting you are doing right now. Round to the nearest half hour and do not be generous to yourself. Then share the profit between those hours. That single number, dollars for one hour of your time, is the one that lets this spring be compared with anything else you could have done with it, and you will meet it again in the Think lane today.
checklist: Every cost from weeks 5, 6 and 7 is on the page with a date and what it bought, ticked off against a receipt or a note
The loan and the float are both on the money in side, labelled in words as a loan and as a float, and neither is written as takings
The takings were worked out twice, from the sale lines and from the cash against the float, and both numbers are written down whether or not they agree
Profit is written as the full sum, takings minus every cost, in pen
My own hours are added up and the profit for one hour of my time is on the page in dollars

figure.alt: Three columns on one sheet, reinvest, save and spend, each filled with the same three rows before anything is circled: what it gives you, what it costs you as the thing given up, and what you would have to be right about.

steps.title: Repay the loan, then argue the decision on paper
steps.body:
The float first, because it was never the shop's money. Count it back out of the box, the same number you wrote down before the stand opened, and give it back to whoever put it in. Write that line on the money out side and call it the float going home, not a cost. What is left in the box is the takings, and now every coin in there was earned.

Then the loan, in cash, by hand, out loud. Count the notes and coins one at a time into a grown up's hand and say the numbers as they go. Then both of you write one line at the bottom of the ledger: the amount, the date, repaid in full, and both signatures. Rule the loan line at the top of the page through, and write repaid beside it.

Do this before the decision, not after, and here is why. Until the float has gone home and the loan is gone, some of the money in that box is somebody else's, and a plan made with somebody else's money in the pile is a plan made on a number that was never yours. What is left once both have gone is the real number, and it should match the profit line if the loan paid for every cost. If you also spent your own money on the shop, take that back too, and now it matches. Two routes to one number again.

Now the decision, and the rule is that it is argued before it is made. Three columns on one sheet: reinvest in a second run, save it, spend it. Every column gets three lines, all three filled in before anything is circled.

Line one: what it gives you. A second run gives more stock and a shot at more profit. Saving gives interest and a bigger number later. Spending gives you the thing you want, now, which is a real answer and not a joke one.

Line two: what it costs you. Not what you hand over: what you give up by choosing it. Choosing the run means the money cannot be earning interest, and it means ten more hours at the workbench that could have been anything at all. Choosing to save means no second run this season. Choosing to spend means the money is gone and the shop is finished. Every yes is a quiet no to something else, and this line is where you write the no.

Line three: what you would have to be right about. The run only pays if people buy the second batch. The saving only pays if you leave it alone. Say the thing each choice is betting on.

Then circle one, date it, sign it, and write one sentence under it saying why. You defend this at the summit in week 12 with the numbers in your hand, so the sentence should be one you would still say to somebody who disagreed.
checklist: The float was counted back out and given to whoever lent it before the loan was touched, and the loan was then counted out in real cash into a hand, out loud
One line at the bottom of the ledger says the amount, the date and repaid in full, signed by both of us
All three columns are filled in completely before any of them is circled
Every column has a line saying what choosing it costs, written as the thing given up rather than the money handed over
The choice is circled, dated, signed, and has one sentence underneath saying why

figure.alt: Three input lines this project's programs expect, each broken into its labelled pieces: a costs.txt line holds a name, a kind and an amount; a demand.txt line holds a price, then shy, likely and bold guesses; a typed sale line holds a count and a price each.

steps.title: Put the shop where a stranger could run it
steps.body:
Week 3 put last season's free build on the internet. Today the shop's own code goes up, and this folder is different in one important way: git has been watching it since week 1, so it already has a trail of camps in it. You are not starting a repo. You are giving one that already exists a home.

A parent signs in to the family GitHub account and stays beside you. Then, in the season folder, in this order:

Run `git status` to see where things stand, and `git log --oneline` to see the trail you have cut since week 1. Read a few of those messages. Some of them are from a version of you who did not know what input did.

Now the part nobody skips. Open every file in that folder and look at it, out loud, one at a time. This is a folder you have been throwing things into for nine weeks, and the moment it goes public, anyone the address reaches can read all of it. Three rules, same as always: no last name, no school name, no street or house number. If a file should not be public, move it out of the folder before the push, not after. Assume that anything published can be copied by anybody who sees it, and that deleting it later does not un-copy it.

Commit anything still uncommitted with `git add .` and a `git commit` whose message says why, not what. Then make a new empty repository on GitHub, with a name that says what it is, in lowercase with hyphens. Do not let GitHub add a README for you; yours is coming. Decide public or private together, out loud, before the click.

Then the three lines the empty repo page prints, in the order it prints them: the `git remote add origin` line that points the folder at its new home, then `git branch -M main`, then `git push -u origin main`. Do not skip the middle one. When it finishes, `git remote -v` shows you where it points, and the address opens in a browser.

Now the README, and this one has a harder job than week 3's. It has to let a stranger run a stand. Five questions, answered in your own words:

1. What is this? Two sentences: a set of programs that ran a real stand for a real day.

2. What do you need? Python 3 and nothing else, and say so.

3. How do I run each program? One numbered list per program, starting from opening the folder, and the exact thing to type: `python cost_sheet.py`, and the note that on some machines the word is python3.

4. What does each one want from me? This is the part week 3's README never needed. Each program reads lines, and a stranger cannot guess the shape of a line. Show one real line of each file and label its pieces: what a line of costs.txt holds, what a line of the demand table holds, and what one sale typed into the tally looks like. One example line is worth a paragraph of description.

5. What should I see? What good output looks like, so a reader can tell working from silently broken.

Then the rehearsal, which is the whole point of a README. Push it, open the page, and read it top to bottom as if you had never seen the project. Hands in your lap. Every place where you had to remember something the page did not say, mark it, fix it, and push again.
checklist: Every file in the folder was opened and looked at before the push, and anything that should not be public was moved out of the folder first
The repository was made empty on GitHub with a parent signed in, and public or private was said out loud before the click
git push finished, and the address opens in a browser and shows the commits with their messages
The README shows one real example line for each input file, with its pieces labelled
Nothing on the page shows my last name, my school or where we live

steps.title: Bug diary
steps.body:
One line each for what did not work the first time and what you tried. Today's usual suspects, and note that most of today's trouble is not in the code.

The two takings numbers disagree. This is the most interesting thing that can happen today and it is not a bug. Write both numbers in the log, write the gap, and write your best honest guess at where it went. A shop whose two routes agree first time has usually just been lucky.

The push is rejected with a message about permission: the browser is signed in but the terminal is not, so the account that owns the repo and the account the terminal is using are two different things. A parent sorts that out with you.

The push says `src refspec main does not match any`: your branch is not called main, so there is no main to send. `git branch -M main` renames it and the push goes.

The push is rejected with a message saying the remote contains work you do not have locally: you let GitHub add a README or a licence when you made the repo, so there is a commit up there that is not on your laptop. The clean fix is to make the repo empty in the first place. If it has already happened, a grown up runs `git pull --rebase origin main` once, and then the push goes.

`git status` says nothing to commit, working tree clean, and you were sure you had changed something: you saved the file somewhere else, or you are in the wrong folder. `pwd` tells you where you actually are.

The README shows your headings as hashes rather than as headings on the page: a hash needs a space after it before the words start.

And the one that is not a bug: the profit came out smaller than it felt like at the stand. It usually does. Money arriving all day is loud, and costs paid weeks ago are quiet, and the ledger is the only place they get to speak at the same volume.

steps.title: Show it
steps.prompt: A photo of the finished ledger page, in pen, with both columns, both takings routes, the profit sum and the profit for one hour of your time. A photo of the repayment line at the bottom with both signatures, with no last names in shot. A photo of the three column decision sheet with one column circled and dated. Plus the README file itself, and the address of the repo written out, so the stranger test in week 12 has somewhere to start.
